claim: Blood vessels are considered an integral component of neural stem cell niches.
source: Blood vessels (BVs) are considered an integral component of neural stem cells (NSCs) niches.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature establishing this concept.

claim: NSCs in the dentate gyrus have enigmatic elaborated apical cellular processes that are associated with blood vessels.
source: NSCs in the dentate gyrus (DG(have enigmatic elaborated apical cellular processes that are associated with BVs.
evidence: Stated as background knowledge in the abstract.

claim: BBB-impermeable fluorescent tracer injected transcardially to mice is selectively uptaken by DG NSCs within a minute.
source: BBB-impermeable fluorescent tracer injected transcardially to mice is selectively uptaken by DG NSCs within a minute, via the vessel-associated apical processes.
evidence: Experimental observation from tracer injection experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: RGL apical processes measured >30 nm in diameter establish direct membrane-to-membrane contact with endothelial cells.
source: These processes, measured >30 nm in diameter, establish direct membrane-to-membrane contact with endothelial cells in specialized areas of irregular endothelial basement membrane and enriched with vesicular activity.
evidence: Based on electron microscopy measurements and observations presented in the manuscript.

claim: RGL-BV contact points occur in specialized areas of irregular endothelial basement membrane.
source: These processes, measured >30 nm in diameter, establish direct membrane-to-membrane contact with endothelial cells in specialized areas of irregular endothelial basement membrane and enriched with vesicular activity.
evidence: Observed through electron microscopy and immunofluorescence imaging.

claim: RGL-BV contact points are enriched with vesicular activity.
source: These processes, measured >30 nm in diameter, establish direct membrane-to-membrane contact with endothelial cells in specialized areas of irregular endothelial basement membrane and enriched with vesicular activity.
evidence: Demonstrated through electron microscopy showing vesicular structures at contact points.

claim: Doxorubicin, a brain-impermeable chemotherapeutic agent, is readily and selectively uptaken by NSCs.
source: Doxorubicin, a brain-impermeable chemotherapeutic agent, is also readily and selectively uptaken by NSCs and reduces their proliferation, which might explain its problematic anti-neurogenic or cognitive side-effect.
evidence: Experimental observation from doxorubicin injection experiments.

claim: Doxorubicin uptake by NSCs reduces their proliferation.
source: Doxorubicin, a brain-impermeable chemotherapeutic agent, is also readily and selectively uptaken by NSCs and reduces their proliferation, which might explain its problematic anti-neurogenic or cognitive side-effect.
evidence: Demonstrated through proliferation assays (Ki67 and BrdU) after doxorubicin treatment.

claim: The NSC-BV communication route explains how circulatory neurogenic mediators are 'sensed' by NSCs.
source: The newly-discovered NSC-BV communication route explains how circulatory neurogenic mediators are 'sensed' by NSCs.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental findings showing direct uptake of blood-borne substances by NSCs.

claim: In the adult rodent brain, NSCs are confined to two locales: the subventricular zone of the lateral ventricles and the DG of the hippocampus.
source: In the adult rodent brain, NSCs are confined into two locales, namely the subventricular zone (SVZ) of the lateral ventricles and the DG of the hippocampus.
evidence: Established knowledge in the field of adult neurogenesis.

claim: DG NSCs proliferate and differentiate into granule cells eventually integrating into the existing network.
source: NSCs within the DG proliferate and differentiate into granule cells (GCs) eventually integrating into the existing network (van Praag et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: DG NSCs are also known as radial-glia-like cells (RGLs).
source: DG NSCs [also known as radial-glia-like cells (RGLs) (Bonaguidi et al., 2011)
evidence: Established terminology supported by citation.

claim: RGLs are distinguished by a unique, tree-like morphology with soma embedded in the subgranular zone.
source: DG NSCs [also known as radial-glia-like cells (RGLs) (Bonaguidi et al., 2011) are distinguished by a unique, tree-like morphology with soma embedded in the subgranular zone (SGZ), a major shaft extending through the adjacent granule cell layer (GCL) and terminating in a dense network of fine cytoplasmic processes spreading in the inner molecular layer (Gebara et al., 2016).
evidence: Morphological description supported by citation.

claim: RGLs have a major shaft extending through the adjacent granule cell layer and terminating in a dense network of fine cytoplasmic processes spreading in the inner molecular layer.
source: DG NSCs [also known as radial-glia-like cells (RGLs) (Bonaguidi et al., 2011) are distinguished by a unique, tree-like morphology with soma embedded in the subgranular zone (SGZ), a major shaft extending through the adjacent granule cell layer (GCL) and terminating in a dense network of fine cytoplasmic processes spreading in the inner molecular layer (Gebara et al., 2016).
evidence: Morphological description supported by citation.

claim: The functional role of RGL terminal shafts has remained obscure.
source: The functional role of these terminal shafts (if any) has remained obscure.
evidence: Statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Blood vessels are considered an integral, indispensable component of stem cell niches, including NSC niches.
source: Blood vessels (BVs) are considered an integral, indispensable component of stem cell niches, including NSC niches (Licht and Keshet, 2015; Schildge et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Blood vessels may impact stem cell performance via locally released blood-borne substances or via paracrinically acting factors elaborated by the endothelium.
source: BV may impact stem cell performance by two different modes: via locally released blood-borne substances or via paracrinically acting factors elaborated by the endothelium ('angiocrine factors')(Rafii et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation describing mechanisms of BV influence on stem cells.

claim: Adult hippocampal RGLs are mostly quiescent but undergo several rounds of cell division upon activation.
source: Adult hippocampal RGLs are mostly quiescent but undergo several rounds of cell division upon activation (Encinas et al., 2011; Pilz et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Neurogenic rates are greatly affected by systemic cues, exemplified by exercise-enhanced neurogenesis shown to be mediated by systemic factors.
source: Neurogenic rates are greatly affected by systemic cues, exemplified by exercise-enhanced neurogenesis shown to be mediated by systemic factors (Fabel et al., 2003; Ma et al., 2017; Moon et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Heterochronic parabiosis experiments have demonstrated reciprocal influences on neurogenic rates mediated by systemic factors such as CCl11 or GDF11.
source: Likewise, heterochronic parabiosis experiments have demonstrated reciprocal influences on neurogenic rates mediated by systemic factors such as CCl11 or GDF11 (Katsimpardi et al., 2014; Villeda et al., 2011; Villeda and Wyss-Coray, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Hippocampal blood vessels, including those of the DG where RGLs reside, are thought to have a fully-functional BBB.
source: Because hippocampal BVs (including those of the DG where RGLs reside) are thought to have a fully-functional BBB, the question arises how are circulating substances accessible to the brain parenchyma without a loss of BBB function?
evidence: Statement of established knowledge in the field.

claim: SVZ-resident type B NSCs and DG-resident RGLs are intimately associated with blood vessels.
source: Both SVZ-resident type B NSCs and DG-resident RGLs were shown to be intimately associated with BVs.
evidence: Statement of prior findings in the field.

claim: In the SVZ, NSCs send a cellular process that wraps a capillary in the nearby striatum.
source: In the SVZ, NSCs send a cellular process that wraps a capillary in the nearby striatum (Lacar et al., 2012; Licht and Keshet, 2015; Mirzadeh et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In the DG, RGLs are physically associated with blood vessels at both the soma side and the apical side.
source: In the DG, RGLs are physically associated with BVs at both the soma side (Filippov et al., 2003; Licht and Keshet, 2015; Palmer et al., 2000) and the apical side (Licht and Keshet, 2015; Licht et al., 2016; Moss et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The functional significance of RGL-BV engagements is not well understood.
source: However, the functional significance of RGL-BV engagements is not well understood.
evidence: Statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Systemically-injected doxorubicin can be uptaken by RGLs and provide a direct anti-mitotic mechanism for its anti-neurogenic effect.
source: Additionally, we show that systemically-injected doxorubicin (a BBB-impermeable DNA-intercalating agent used for non-cerebral tumors) can be uptaken by RGLs and provide a direct anti-mitotic mechanism for its anti-neurogenic effect.
evidence: Demonstrated through doxorubicin injection experiments and proliferation assays.

claim: Previous studies using Nestin-GFP to label RGLs were limited because mural pericytes are also labeled by this reporter.
source: Previous studies that used Nestin-GFP to label RGLs (Filippov et al., 2003; Moss et al., 2016) were limited by the fact that mural pericytes are also labeled by this reporter (see Figure 1a; Nakazato et al., 2017), which makes perivascular pericytes and RGLs indistinguishable at the electron microscopy (EM) level.
evidence: Supported by citation and reference to Figure 1a showing pericyte labeling.

claim: Gli1-creERT2 mice express inducible Cre exclusively in RGLs and not in other DG cells.
source: To overcome this shortcoming, we used Gli1-creERT2 mice [a mouse line in which inducible Cre is not expressed in DG cells other than RGLs (Ahn and Joyner, 2004) crossed to Ai9 (TdTomato) reporter line.
evidence: Supported by citation describing the mouse line properties.

claim: RGL processes can be as thin as 30 nm in diameter.
source: At the inner molecular layer in the vicinity of those soma, we identified capillaries that are tightly wrapped by extra-fine (as thin as 30 nm in diameter) RGL processes labeled with DAB (Figure 1d–g).
evidence: Measured from electron microscopy images shown in Figure 1.

claim: The basement membrane is visualized in EM images as a grayish 50–100 nm-thick layer surrounding the abluminal aspect of endothelial cells.
source: The BM is visualized in EM images as a grayish 50–100 nm-thick layer surrounding the abluminal aspect of endothelial cells (Figure 2a).
evidence: Description of EM imaging characteristics with reference to Figure 2a.

claim: The basement membrane thoroughly encircles DG capillaries of the hilus and outer molecular layer.
source: This component was found to thoroughly encircle DG capillaries of the hilus and outer molecular layer.
evidence: Observation from electron microscopy imaging.

claim: Engagement of RGL processes with blood vessels takes place in endothelial surfaces distinguished by irregular BM structures.
source: Strikingly, however, observing endothelial-RGL processes contact points in the inner molecular layer revealed that engagement with BVs takes place in endothelial surfaces distinguished by irregular BM structures (absence of a classical BM appearance), thus allowing for possible direct membrane-to-membrane contact without the barrier imposed by the BM (Figure 2b).
evidence: Observed through electron microscopy shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Only approximately 30% of vessel abluminal aspect in contact with RGL retain the typical BM structure.
source: Based on TEM images, we quantified BM coverage at RGL contact points in comparison to areas devoid of RGL and found a significant difference (Fig, 2 c). Only ~30% of vessel abluminal aspect in contact with RGL retain the typical BM structure (as shown in Figure 2c right).
evidence: Quantified from TEM images as shown in Figure 2c.

claim: There is a significant difference in BM coverage at RGL contact points compared to areas devoid of RGL.
source: Based on TEM images, we quantified BM coverage at RGL contact points in comparison to areas devoid of RGL and found a significant difference (Fig, 2 c).
evidence: Statistical analysis of quantified TEM images shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Laminin immunofluorescence is reduced where RGL processes contact blood vessels.
source: We analyzed images of Gli+ RFP-labeled RGLs in contact with blood vessels (Figure 3c–i) and found reduced laminin immunofluorescence where RGLs processes were present.
evidence: Observed through confocal and super-resolution microscopy shown in Figure 3.

claim: Vessels in the DG not in contact with RGLs and cortical vessels have more pronounced laminin immunofluorescence compared to RGL-BV contact points.
source: In comparison, vessels in the DG not in contact with RGLs (Figure 3j,k) and cortical vessels (Figure 3l,m) had more pronounced laminin immunofluorescence.
evidence: Observed through super-resolution microscopy shown in Figure 3.

claim: Quantification of dSTORM laminin signals revealed reduced laminin abundance at vessels with RGL contact compared to DG vessels without RGL or cortical vessels.
source: Quantification of dSTORM laminin signals (normalized to vessel wall length) revealed reduced laminin abundance at vessels which included a contact point with RGL in comparison with DG vessels without RGL process or in comparison with cortical vessels (Figure 3n).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of super-resolution microscopy images shown in Figure 3n.

claim: Collagen IV expression is reduced in areas of RGL-BV contact.
source: Immunofluorescence for a second major protein of the BM, namely collagen IV, also revealed an apparent reduction in its expression in areas of RGL-BV contact (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Observed through immunofluorescence shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The BV-RGL interface is characterized by robust vesicular activity with many cytoplasmic and abluminal membrane-bound vesicular-like structures measured 60–100 nm in diameter.
source: The BV-RGL interface was also characterized by robust vesicular activity as many cytoplasmic and abluminal membrane-bound vesicular-like structures (measured 60–100 nm in diameter) were detected there (Figure 4a–c and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Observed and measured from electron microscopy images shown in Figure 4.

claim: TEM images of capillaries at the inner molecular layer revealed luminal, cytoplasmic and abluminal vesicles containing HRP.
source: TEM images of capillaries at the inner molecular layer revealed luminal, cytoplasmic and abluminal vesicles containing HRP (Figure 4d,e).
evidence: Observed from HRP injection experiments and TEM imaging shown in Figure 4.

claim: The density of HRP-containing vesicles at the BM-modified RGL-BV interface is greater compared to BV segments without RGL or BV-RGL interface separated by a clear BM.
source: The density of these vesicles (vesicles/length of the abluminal boundary (μm)) at the BM-modified RGL-BV interface was greater in comparison with BV segments which did not contain an RGL as well as with BV-RGL interface separated by a clear BM (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c,d).
evidence: Quantified from electron microscopy images shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: A fluorescently-tagged 10Kd dextran tracer is fully contained in the lumen of blood vessels with a functional BBB.
source: To examine the possibility that other cells in the intact adult brain are 'privileged' in the sense of having access to blood-borne substances, we injected into the systemic circulation a fluorescently-tagged 10Kd dextran tracer previously shown to be fully contained in the lumen of blood vessels with a functional BBB (Ben-Zvi et al., 2014; Licht et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research establishing tracer properties.

claim: With the exception of the median eminence of the hypothalamus and choroid plexus vessels, the 10Kd dextran tracer is fully retained in nearly all other cerebral blood vessels.
source: Inspection of cryosections, co-stained with CD31 to highlight BVs, confirmed that - with the exception of the median eminence of the hypothalamus (a circumventricular organ) and choroid plexus vessels which are known to lack a functional BBB - the tracer is indeed fully retained in nearly all other cerebral BVs (Figure 5a).
evidence: Observed from tracer injection experiments shown in Figure 5a.

claim: A small population of cells in the DG was labeled with the 10Kd dextran tracer.
source: As expected, a small population of cells in the DG was labeled (Figure 5a, top left, and Figure 5b).
evidence: Observed from tracer injection experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Tracer-labeled cells in the DG have their soma located in the SGZ and a major shaft extended towards the molecular layer.
source: These cells had their soma located in the SGZ, i.e., coinciding with the region where RGLs soma reside, and a major shaft extended towards the molecular layer.
evidence: Observed from tracer injection experiments and microscopy.

claim: The location and unique morphology of tracer-labeled cells strongly suggest that these are DG RGLs.
source: In fact, both the location and unique morphology of tracer-labeled cells strongly suggested that these are DG RGLs.
evidence: Inferred from morphological characteristics and location of labeled cells.

claim: There is a clear continuum in tracer presence from the vessel through the major shaft to the soma with no apparent signs of extracellular spillage.
source: As shown in Figure 5c, there is a clear continuum in tracer presence from the vessel through the major shaft to the soma with no apparent signs of extracellular spillage.
evidence: Observed from 3D reconstructions of confocal images shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The tracer accumulates mostly in the major shaft and soma of RGLs, with barely visible signal in the tree-like processes.
source: As shown in Figure 6a, due to their fineness, the tracer was barely visible in the tree-like processes and most of it accumulated in the major shaft and soma.
evidence: Observed from tracer injection experiments in Nestin-GFP mice shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Biotinylated tracer co-localizes with nestin-GFP RGLs in both the soma and the apical processes.
source: Co-localization of biotinylated tracer with nestin-GFP RGLs was evident in both the soma and the apical processes (Figure 6b).
evidence: Observed from biotin-labeled tracer experiments shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Doxorubicin is a widely-used chemotherapeutic agent of the Anthracyclines family of DNA-intercalating agents.
source: Doxorubicin (dox) is a widely-used chemotherapeutic agent of the Anthracyclines family of DNA -intercalating agents.
evidence: Established knowledge about doxorubicin.

claim: Inaccessibility of doxorubicin to the brain parenchyma has precluded its use for treating brain tumors.
source: While inaccessibility of this small molecule (543 Da) to the brain parenchyma (Ohnishi et al., 1995; Treat et al., 2007) has precluded its use for treating brain tumors, its use against other tumors is often associated with significant cognitive impairment, also known as 'chemo brain' (reviewed by El-Agamy et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Doxorubicin use against non-cerebral tumors is often associated with significant cognitive impairment, also known as 'chemo brain'.
source: While inaccessibility of this small molecule (543 Da) to the brain parenchyma (Ohnishi et al., 1995; Treat et al., 2007) has precluded its use for treating brain tumors, its use against other tumors is often associated with significant cognitive impairment, also known as 'chemo brain' (reviewed by El-Agamy et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Findings in rodents show that doxorubicin has a dramatic negative effect on DG neurogenesis.
source: Findings in rodents showing that dox have a dramatic negative effect on DG neurogenesis (Christie et al., 2012; Janelsins et al., 2010; Kitamura et al., 2015; Park et al., 2018) prompted us to examine whether this seemingly paradoxical situation could be explained by direct selective uptake of systemically-administered dox by RGLs.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Doxorubicin has the same fluorescent properties as commonly used red fluorophores.
source: Here we took advantage of the fact that dox have the same fluorescent properties as commonly used red fluorophores thereby enabling its direct visualization in cell nuclei in PFA-fixed brain sections.
evidence: Statement of known chemical property of doxorubicin.

claim: Systemically-injected doxorubicin does not cross to brain parenchyma in regions with a functional BBB.
source: The fact that systemically-injected dox does not cross to brain parenchyma was validated by showing that in all brain regions known to have a functional BBB, dox was detected only in endothelial cell nuclei (exemplified for the cortex and CA1 region of the hippocampus in Figure 7a)
evidence: Observed from doxorubicin injection experiments shown in Figure 7a.

claim: In brain areas where the BBB is inactive, doxorubicin-labeled nuclei are readily detected outside the vasculature.
source: whereas in areas in which the BBB is inactive, dox-labeled nuclei were also readily detected outside the vasculature (shown for the choroid plexus and the median eminence of the hypothalamus in Figure 7a).
evidence: Observed from doxorubicin injection experiments shown in Figure 7a.

claim: Doxorubicin uptake by RGLs is evidenced by significant labeling of RGL nuclei within 1–2 min from its injection into the circulation.
source: An outstanding exception was dox uptake by RGLs, evidenced by significant labeling of RGL nuclei within 1–2 min from its injection into the circulation of nestin-GFP mice where co-labeling with GFP confirmed the RGL identity of dox-uptaking cells (Figure 7b and c).
evidence: Observed from doxorubicin injection experiments in Nestin-GFP mice shown in Figure 7.

claim: Doxorubicin treatment did not affect the total numbers of Nestin+ RGL population.
source: Dox treatment did not have an effect on the total numbers of Nestin+ RGL population (Figure 8b, right), as the majority of those cells are not proliferating.
evidence: Quantified from immunofluorescence experiments shown in Figure 8b.

claim: The numbers of proliferating RGLs decreased significantly following doxorubicin treatment as measured by Ki67 and BrdU.
source: We immunostained for both the proliferation marker Ki67 (Figure 8b) and for BrdU (Figure 8c) to detect the proliferating RGL populations. In both cases, the numbers of proliferating RGLs have decreased significantly following dox treatment (Figure 8b and c).
evidence: Quantified from immunofluorescence experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: A direct antimitotic effect of doxorubicin is a presumable explanation for reduced neurogenesis reported in rodents treated with doxorubicin.
source: We, therefore, suggest a direct antimitotic effect of dox as a presumable explanation for reduced neurogenesis reported in rodents treated with dox and as a possible factor in the 'chemo-brain' side effect of cancer patients.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental findings showing doxorubicin uptake and reduced proliferation.

claim: The direct uptake of blood-borne molecules by RGLs provides a mechanistic explanation to systemic influences on adult hippocampal neurogenesis.
source: We conclude that this unique NVU pathway may serve as a gateway for molecules that need to bypass the barrier or a 'hole in the fence' allowing for penetration of molecules that should not enter the brain. We believe that the new mode of delivery of systemic molecules to RGLs uncovered by this study, not only provides a mechanistic explanation to systemic influences on adult hippocampal neurogenesis but may also provide new means of interventional modulations of this important process.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental findings showing direct uptake pathway.

claim: The unique NVU pathway may serve as a gateway for molecules that need to bypass the barrier.
source: We conclude that this unique NVU pathway may serve as a gateway for molecules that need to bypass the barrier or a 'hole in the fence' allowing for penetration of molecules that should not enter the brain.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental findings and speculated about broader implications.

claim: The unique NVU pathway may provide new means of interventional modulations of adult hippocampal neurogenesis.
source: We believe that the new mode of delivery of systemic molecules to RGLs uncovered by this study, not only provides a mechanistic explanation to systemic influences on adult hippocampal neurogenesis but may also provide new means of interventional modulations of this important process.
evidence: Speculated potential application based on the findings.

claim: Circulatory molecules shown to increase or decrease neurogenesis include specific cytokines whose circulatory levels change with age.
source: Circulatory molecules were shown to increase (or decrease) neurogenesis include specific cytokines whose circulatory levels change with age, as well as blood components accumulating in plasma following physical exercise and shown to upregulate DG neurogenesis (Castellano et al., 2017; Cooper et al., 2018; Fabel et al., 2003; Leiter et al., 2019; Ozek et al., 2018; Smith et al., 2015; Villeda et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Blood components accumulating in plasma following physical exercise upregulate DG neurogenesis.
source: Circulatory molecules were shown to increase (or decrease) neurogenesis include specific cytokines whose circulatory levels change with age, as well as blood components accumulating in plasma following physical exercise and shown to upregulate DG neurogenesis (Castellano et al., 2017; Cooper et al., 2018; Fabel et al., 2003; Leiter et al., 2019; Ozek et al., 2018; Smith et al., 2015; Villeda et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Additional physiologic cues impacting DG neurogenesis are likely mediated by systemic factors making use of the direct gateway to DG RGLs.
source: It is likely that additional physiologic cues impacting DG neurogenesis are also mediated by systemic factors making use of this direct gateway to DG RGLs.
evidence: Speculated based on the findings about the direct uptake pathway.

claim: The transfer of blood-borne molecules to RGL cell bodies takes place through RGL's thin cytoplasmic processes.
source: Our finding showing that the transfer of blood-borne molecules to RGL cell bodies takes place through RGL's thin cytoplasmic processes ascribes a first known function to the obscure terminal arbor of RGLs.
evidence: Demonstrated through tracer experiments showing continuum from vessel to soma.

claim: SVZ NSCs failed to uptake injected molecules despite contacting blood vessels via a single extended process.
source: Noteworthy, unlike RGLs, SVZ NSCs failed to uptake injected molecules (Figure 5a) despite the fact that they also contact BV via a single extended process (Mirzadeh et al., 2008).
evidence: Observed from tracer injection experiments shown in Figure 5a and compared to prior knowledge.

claim: VEGF-promoted BV rejuvenation leads to remodeling of the terminal RGL arbor and engagement with more remote capillaries.
source: Moreover, we showed that VEGF-promoted BV rejuvenation leads to remodeling of the terminal RGL arbor and engagement with even more remote capillaries (Licht et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: The fine processes of RGLs in the DG make direct contact with the membrane of nearby endothelial cells in the inner molecular layer.
source: We show, using EM imaging, that the fine processes of RGLs in the DG make direct contact with the membrane of nearby endothelial cell in the inner molecular layer.
evidence: Demonstrated through electron microscopy imaging.

claim: RGL-endothelial cell contact takes place in areas with modified/reduced endothelial basement membrane.
source: This contact takes place in areas with modified/reduced endothelial BM, as shown by both EM imaging and immunofluorescence/super-resolution microscopy.
evidence: Demonstrated through multiple imaging modalities.

claim: BBB vasculature is known to be poor in vesicular activity.
source: While BBB vasculature is known to be poor in vesicular activity (Ben-Zvi et al., 2014), these findings suggest that this unique connection may allow for systemic molecules to be delivered via vesicular transcytosis directly to the membrane of RGLs.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The unique RGL-BV connection may allow for systemic molecules to be delivered via vesicular transcytosis directly to the membrane of RGLs.
source: While BBB vasculature is known to be poor in vesicular activity (Ben-Zvi et al., 2014), these findings suggest that this unique connection may allow for systemic molecules to be delivered via vesicular transcytosis directly to the membrane of RGLs.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of vesicular activity at RGL-BV contact points.

claim: Doxorubicin is a substrate for p-glycoprotein pumps and is not available to the brain.
source: However, it has been difficult to reconcile the adverse cerebral side effects of dox with the fact that it is a substrate for p-glycoprotein pumps and is not available to the brain.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about doxorubicin.

claim: The finding that systemically-injected doxorubicin is readily uptaken by DG RGLs provides a more compelling explanation to its adverse cerebral side effects than previous suggestions of indirect mechanisms.
source: Our finding that systemically-injected dox is readily and efficiently uptaken by DG RGLs provides a more compelling explanation to this seeming paradox than previous suggestions arguing an indirect mechanism mediated by secondary molecules (Janelsins et al., 2010; Kitamura et al., 2015).
evidence: Inferred from the experimental findings showing direct uptake, contrasted with prior hypotheses.

claim: Treatment with doxorubicin decreases proliferating RGL numbers, suggesting a cell-autonomous anti-mitotic mechanism.
source: We show here that the treatment by dox decreases proliferating RGL numbers thus suggesting a cell-autonomous anti-mitotic mechanism.
evidence: Demonstrated through proliferation assays and inferred mechanism.

claim: In Nestin-GFP mice, both RGLs and pericytes are GFP-labeled.
source: In this line, both RGLs and pericytes (arrows) are GFP-labeled.
evidence: Stated in the figure legend for Figure 1a.

claim: RGLs have contact points with blood vessels at both the basal side at the SGZ and the apical side at the inner molecular layer.
source: Please note the contact points of RGLs and blood vessels at both the basal side at the SGZ (1) and the apical side at the inner molecular layer (2).
evidence: Described in the figure legend for Figure 1a.

claim: Only RGLs are labeled in the DG of Gli1-CreERT2 crossed to Ai9 mouse line.
source: Note that only RGLs are labeled in the DG of this mouse line.
evidence: Stated in the figure legend for Figure 1b.

claim: The basement membrane has a double-layered structure at pericyte contact points.
source: Please note a double-layered BM at the pericyte (P) contact point and a clear BM at the contact point with an astrocyte (A).
evidence: Observed in electron microscopy images shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The basement membrane has a clear structure at astrocyte contact points.
source: Please note a double-layered BM at the pericyte (P) contact point and a clear BM at the contact point with an astrocyte (A).
evidence: Observed in electron microscopy images shown in Figure 2a.

claim: There is no characteristic basement membrane at the contact point of RGL with the endothelial cell.
source: Note no characteristic BM at the contact point of RGL (R) with the endothelial cell (E).
evidence: Observed in electron microscopy images shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Laminin signal in dSTORM images at DG vessels with RGL contact is significantly lower than at DG vessels without RGL contact (p=0.005).
source: F(2,29) = 8.221, p=0.001. Post hoc analysis: DG w/RGL vs. DG wo/RGL: p=0.005.
evidence: Statistical analysis of quantified super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 3n.

claim: Laminin signal in dSTORM images at DG vessels with RGL contact is significantly lower than at cortical vessels (p=0.019).
source: DG w/RGL vs cortex: p=0.019.
evidence: Statistical analysis of quantified super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 3n.

claim: Collagen IV staining is reduced at BV-RGL contact points.
source: Note reduced Collagen IV staining at the contact points (arrows).
evidence: Observed in immunofluorescence images shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: HRP-filled vesicles are increased at the contact point with an RGL with modified/vague BM appearance.
source: Increased HRP-filled vesicles (arrows) at the contact point with an RGL (R) with modified\vague BM apparence.
evidence: Observed in electron microscopy images shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Vesicle density at capillaries with no RGL is significantly lower than at capillaries with RGL without BM (p=0.001).
source: F(2,46)=16.839 p=3.25*10−6. Post hoc analysis: No RGL vs. RGL without BM p=0.001.
evidence: Statistical analysis of quantified electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Vesicle density at capillaries with RGL and BM is significantly lower than at capillaries with RGL without BM (p=3.19*10−6).
source: RGL with BM vs. RGL without BM p=3.19*10−6.
evidence: Statistical analysis of quantified electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1d.

claim: The tracer did not infiltrate into cells outside of the vasculature except for a specific population of cells in the SGZ of the DG, the choroid plexus, and the median eminence of the hypothalamus.
source: Tracer did not infiltrate into cells outside of the vasculature except for a specific population of cells in the SGZ of the DG (arrows), the CP and the median eminence of the hypothalamus (arrow).
evidence: Observed from tracer injection experiments shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Labeled SGZ cells have a radial process that is associated with local blood vessels in the inner molecular layer.
source: Labeled SGZ cells have a radial process that is associated with local blood vessels in the inner molecular layer (arrows).

claim: 3D reconstruction of dextran-labeled cells shows mutual contact with capillaries with no labeling of the extracellular space.

claim: Tracer distribution is evident throughout all RGL processes and soma.

claim: In areas with non-barriered endothelium such as the choroid plexus and the median eminence, doxorubicin is detected externally to blood vessels.
